items.title: Your blood sugar is regulated within a 30% range despite irregular meals
items.claim: Normal fasting blood glucose: 4-6 mmol/L. After a meal: rises to 7-8, then back to baseline within 2 hours. Healthy people maintain this range whether they eat constantly or fast for a day.

options.text: Insulin (from pancreatic beta cells) lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake and storage; glucagon (from alpha cells) raises it by mobilising stored glycogen — a classic antagonistic pair under negative feedback

items.reveal:
After a meal: blood glucose rises. Beta cells in the pancreas detect it via glucokinase and secrete insulin. Insulin tells muscle and fat to take up glucose, and the liver to store it as glycogen.

Between meals: glucose drops. Alpha cells secrete glucagon. Glucagon tells the liver to break down glycogen and release glucose into the blood. If glycogen runs out (after ~24 hours fasting), gluconeogenesis from amino acids and glycerol takes over.

Type 1 diabetes: autoimmune destruction of beta cells. No insulin. Blood glucose unregulated. Discovered to be treatable with injected insulin by Banting and Best (1921, Nobel 1923) — life expectancy of Type 1 patients went from months to decades within a year of insulin's availability.

Type 2 diabetes: insulin RESISTANCE develops in target tissues. Beta cells initially compensate (more insulin) then eventually fail. Affects ~10% of adults globally. Strongly linked to obesity and inactivity.

The brain is unique in burning glucose nearly exclusively (~120 g/day, 20% of total body glucose use) — which is why hypoglycaemia causes confusion, seizures and unconsciousness within minutes.
items.why: Hormones feel like signals from somewhere distant. In glucose regulation, two opposing hormones from the same gland keep blood sugar within a tight band — a textbook example of antagonistic negative feedback.

items.title: The most abundant enzyme on Earth is bad at its job
items.claim: Rubisco fixes carbon dioxide into sugar in every photosynthesising organism. It's the most abundant protein on the planet (about half a kilogram in every square metre of leaf). It's also slow (3 reactions per second per active site) and confuses CO2 with O2.
items.prompt: Why do plants invest so heavily in such a flawed enzyme?

options.text: There's no alternative — Rubisco is the only carbon-fixation enzyme that works

Rubisco evolved when the atmosphere had little O2; the confusion between CO2 and O2 was rare then. Now plants mass-produce it (often 50 percent of leaf protein) to compensate for its slowness, and C4 plants concentrate CO2 around it to outcompete O2 binding
Rubisco is highly efficient — the textbook is wrong

items.reveal:
Rubisco's active site binds CO2 by inserting it into a bound substrate (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate). About 25 percent of the time at room temperature, it grabs O2 instead — initiating photorespiration, a wasteful cycle that costs energy and releases CO2.

This was tolerable in the Proterozoic atmosphere (low O2, high CO2). As oxygen rose and CO2 dropped, the problem grew.

C4 plants (corn, sugarcane) evolved an extra carbon-fixation step in mesophyll cells (using PEP carboxylase, which doesn't confuse O2). This shuttles CO2 into specialised bundle-sheath cells at high concentration, where Rubisco then operates without interference.

CAM plants (cacti, pineapples) do the same trick temporally — fixing CO2 at night when stomata can be open without losing water.
items.why: Evolution doesn't engineer optimal enzymes — it tinkers around constraints inherited from earlier conditions. Rubisco is a beautiful example of a molecular legacy system.

items.title: Most adult humans can't digest milk — and that's normal
items.claim: Babies make lactase to digest lactose in milk. In most of the world's adults, lactase production switches off after weaning. Adult milk-drinkers — common in Europeans and some African and Middle Eastern populations — carry a recently evolved mutation.

options.text: Adult lactose intolerance is ancestral; lactase persistence is a derived trait that arose in populations that domesticated dairy animals in the last 10,000 years

items.reveal:
Roughly 65 percent of adult humans globally show reduced lactase production after weaning. Lactase persistence is most common in northern Europeans (around 90 percent), some West African pastoralist groups, and some Middle Eastern populations.

Different regulatory mutations independently produced this trait in different lineages — convergent evolution. The European variant (a single nucleotide change near the LCT gene, called T-13910) is dated to about 5,000 to 10,000 years ago, coinciding with cattle domestication.

Dairy farming and lactase persistence appear to have co-evolved: ancient DNA shows farmers drank milk before persistence was common, suggesting cultural use (fermented dairy, lower lactose) preceded biological adaptation. As populations relied more on milk, the persistence allele was strongly selected.
items.why: European diets are taken as a baseline; lactose intolerance is treated as a disorder. Globally, lactose intolerance IS the baseline — milk drinking adults are the rare ones.
